title: Frontier results, on device - RL Nabors, Arize

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on evaluation methodology—capability evals, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge, and regression evals—as the primary lens for model selection and validation. The evaluation framework applies broadly to any AI application rather than targeting a specific vertical. Covers prototyping with frontier models, evaluating candidates via capability evals, deploying small models, and monitoring quality through regression evals. Prerequisites are basic LLM familiarity and JSON knowledge, targeting intermediate practitioners. Conference presentation with a live case study demonstrating the Mima thread-summarization workflow. Claims are supported by demonstrated experiments with quantitative results comparing five models and five prompt variants.

summary: Rachel Lee Nabors frames the true cost of defaulting to frontier models: security exposure, latency beyond a 4-second user-believability threshold, uncontrollable third-party pricing, and total failure when offline. Token prices are falling but total inference spend is rising because agentic reasoning workloads consume tokens faster than prices drop. The solution is task-specific models and Small Language Models (SLMs) for jobs not requiring frontier-scale knowledge. SLMs contain millions to billions of parameters, can be quantized to 8-bit or 4-bit, and consume roughly 25% of the energy of an LLM for the same task. The guiding principle is 'prototype big, deploy small': prove feasibility with the most capable model, then convert to SLMs for production. Using Mima's thread-summarization feature, Nabors prototyped with Claude, exported a golden dataset of 14 threads (28 examples), defined evaluation dimensions, and selected Phoenix for measurement. The capability eval compared Claude Sonnet as baseline against Qwen 2.5 Instruct (1.5B), Qwen 3 (1.7B), Llama 3.2 (3B), and Gemma 4 E2B (5B). Llama 3.2 won at ~90% accuracy with good latency. Nabors introduces the SAGE principle—select the Small And Good Enough Model. Five prompt variants were tested on Llama 3.2; few-shot performed best, improving accuracy with only +200ms latency. Post-processing closed the remaining gap, achieving 100% JSON and structural validity, P50 ~1s, P95 under 3.5s. LLM-as-judge bias was discovered: Claude favored Claude Sonnet over Llama 3.2 in factual consistency scoring. After shipping, Nabors stresses regression evals—run like CI/CD tests—to catch regressions when prompts or models are updated, preventing accidental breakage. The talk closes with a challenge to audit which frontier calls could be local calls, noting Chrome's built-in Gemini Nano via the Prompt API as a zero-shipping option. The four-step process is recapped: prove it, define it, test it, select your SAGE model. Resources include Phoenix at phoenix.arize.com and the Mima beta at mima.social.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Frontier-model inference carries hidden costs in security, latency, offline failure, and rising total spend despite falling token prices.
Follow 'prototype big, deploy small': prove feasibility with the most capable model, then replace with smaller models for production.
Select the SAGE model—the Small And Good Enough Model—by testing from small to large against your own golden dataset, not external benchmarks.
Few-shot prompting is often the most effective prompt-engineering technique for small models, improving accuracy with minimal latency cost.
Post-processing in the harness can close remaining gaps that prompt engineering cannot, handling reference validation and length truncation deterministically.
LLM-as-judge can show bias toward models from the same family; crack open eval results to verify judgments rather than trusting aggregate scores.
Run regression evals like CI/CD tests to catch quality regressions when updating prompts or upgrading models after shipping.
Chrome's built-in Gemini Nano via the Prompt API lets you use an on-device model without shipping one to users.
Vocabulary to reason about model performance: capability evals, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge, P50/P95 latency, regression evals
Framework for deciding when a small or local model can replace a frontier model

sections.title: Speaker introduction and the cost of frontier inference
sections.summary: Nabors introduces her background (Mozilla, W3C, Edge, React, Arize) and frames the core problem: every frontier-model call costs in security, latency (4-second believability limit), business (uncontrollable third-party pricing), and offline productivity. Token prices are falling but total inference spend is rising due to agentic reasoning workloads.

sections.title: Small Language Models and task-specific models as alternatives
sections.summary: Introduces SLMs (millions to billions of parameters vs. trillions for LLMs) and task-specific models for vision, audio, and text. Covers quantization benefits, on-device deployment, and the finding that SLMs are production-ready for agentic workloads per 2025 Nvidia research.

sections.title: Energy comparison and benefits of local models
sections.summary: Presents energy bar chart: LLM task at 100%, SLM at ~25%, task-specific at ~12.5%. Lists benefits of local models: secure, offline-capable, no fees, efficient, lower latency. Demonstrates Goose running Gemma locally for a reasoning question.

sections.title: Prototype big, deploy small framework and Mima case study setup
sections.summary: Introduces the 'prototype big, deploy small' framework. Demonstrates with Mima: prototyped thread summarization with Claude, exported a golden dataset of 14 threads (28 examples), defined evaluation dimensions, and selected Phoenix for measurement.

sections.title: Capability eval: comparing Claude Sonnet against small models
sections.summary: Runs a capability eval comparing Claude Sonnet (baseline: 2.9s latency, $0.22 per 14 tasks, ~$1/day) against Qwen 2.5 Instruct (1.5B, 1GB, fastest at ~1s but low accuracy), Qwen 3 (1.7B), Llama 3.2 (3B, 2GB, ~90% accuracy, the winner), and Gemma 4 E2B (5B, 3.1GB, ~8s latency). Introduces the SAGE principle: select the Small And Good Enough Model. Local models cost zero per inference since compute runs on the user's device.

sections.title: Four-step right-sizing process
sections.summary: Outlines the four-step model right-sizing process: (1) prove it's possible with the largest model, (2) set success criteria with a golden dataset, (3) test from small to large against criteria, (4) select the SAGE model. Notes that prompt engineering is the tool for closing gaps when you can't control or update the model on a user's device.

sections.title: Prompt engineering to close the accuracy gap
sections.summary: Tests five prompt variants on Llama 3.2: baseline (ref accuracy 91.2%, factual 87.1%, 1s), numbered input (no improvement), few-shot (best performer, +200ms), strict rules (worse—model resisted negative constraints), and chain-of-thought (slight improvement but +600ms). Few-shot won by improving length accuracy and reference consistency with minimal latency cost.

sections.title: Post-processing and LLM-as-judge bias to close the final gap
sections.summary: After few-shot prompting, Llama 3.2 reached structural validity 91.7% and factual consistency 92.9%. Inspecting individual evals revealed Claude-as-judge was biased toward Claude Sonnet over Llama. Post-processing in the harness (reference count validation, length truncation) closed remaining gaps. Final results: 100% JSON validity, 100% structural validity, P50 ~1s, P95 under 3.5s, meeting and beating Claude's baseline.

sections.title: Regression evals, Chrome Gemini Nano, and call to action
sections.summary: Nabors stresses regression evals—run like CI/CD tests—to catch regressions when prompts or models are updated, citing a true story of a CTO accidentally breaking a founder's agentic experience. Challenges the audience to audit which frontier calls could be local calls and estimate savings. Highlights Chrome's built-in Gemini Nano via the Prompt API as a zero-shipping on-device option, keeping PII on device and saving energy. Recaps the four-step process (prove, define, test, select SAGE) and the 'prototype big, deploy small' principle. Shares resources: nearestneighbors.com, phoenix.arize.com, and mima.social beta. Closes with 'Go forth and build your own inference stack.'
